summary: Plumas NF lookout in Sierra County; first L-4 ground house dated 1933 by NHLR (1932 brochure, 1934 press). Staffed per NHLR; restored and reactivated 2005 per NHLR.

facts.design: First lookout was an L-4 ground house (NHLR); the current structure is described as a tower with stairs, a platform and a compact cab (Calexplornia)

access.note: Entry to the cab may depend on staffing, fire conditions and posted rules; ask before entering

visit.trail_note: About 3 miles of dirt road to the tower; NHLR visitor comment says a car can make the route, while Calexplornia recommends a high-clearance vehicle for the narrow last stretch

events.note: NHLR build year for the first Mills Peak Lookout, an L-4 ground house

Ben Hankey moved to the new lookout at Mills Peak from Mount Elwell (article dated August 2, 1934); 1946 item says construction completed August 1934

T.L. Louton in charge; Forest Service counted 1,520 visitors that season

NHLR: recently restored and reactivated for fire detection in 2005

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR says 1933; an older Forest Service brochure, as reported by Calexplornia, says 1932; 1934 press items describe a new lookout completed in August 1934. Story gives the early 1930s and says the sources disagree.
NHLR and the brochure give 7,342 feet; a 1960 press item gives 7,374 feet. The 7,342-foot figure is kept to match the record.
NHLR visitor comment says a car can make the whole route; Calexplornia says high clearance is advised. Both are recorded in visit.trail_note.

notes_for_editor: Record built year 1933 matches NHLR, so no correction was made. Record kind 'enclosed_tower' could not be confirmed or refuted: the visitor guide describes stairs, a platform and a cab, and NHLR describes the first lookout as a ground house. Staffing comes from the NHLR form field and comment; the Calexplornia staffing claims were not verified and are not used. The NHLR entry dates 2004 yet mentions 2005 restoration; this is not explained in any read source. Calexplornia is a visitor blog; used only for the brochure date and visit conditions. The early-1930s date is the visitor guide's conclusion from the three disagreeing sources, and the story now attributes it that way. No photos added.
